title: High availability: surviving a failure

kcs.statement: High availability means designing a workload to minimise downtime so it keeps meeting its availability target when components fail; a common technique is running redundant copies in independent locations, which in AWS means multiple Availability Zones.

Redundancy only gives high availability when traffic fails over automatically, the data is available in the surviving location and the remaining capacity can carry the load; horizontal scaling within one location adds capacity for more load but does not by itself make a workload highly available.

problem_ideas: An app runs on 4 servers in one data center that loses power: is it highly available? What change fixes it?
Find the single point of failure in a diagram: web servers in two locations, but one database in only one of them.
A company scales from 2 to 8 servers in the same room: did availability, scalability or both improve?
Choose between 'bigger server' and 'second server in another location' for a requirement to survive a building outage.
Compute the uptime gain when two independent locations each have 99% availability (1 - 0.01^2), then say what failover must work for that figure to hold.
Two locations each run at 80% load: explain why losing one still causes an outage despite the redundancy.
